knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

## Load packages 


```{r, warning = FALSE, message= FALSE}

library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)  # help reduce output to specified decimal places
library(ggResidpanel)
```


## Read the Dataset
```{r}
surgery <- read.csv(file.choose())

``` 


```{r}
head(surgery)
```

## Part 1: Fit the linear model
```{r}
fit.surgery <- lm(survival ~ ., data = surgery)

fit.surgery
```

## Part 2: Model Diagnostics 1
### Check for Linearity, Normality and Constant Variance
* Linearity & Constant Variance -use Residual plot
* Normality -use Q-Q Plot

```{r}
plot1 <- resid_panel(fit.surgery, plots = c('resid', 'qq'))

plot1

```

### Results 2.1
* The **Linearity Assumption was not violated:** The residuals on the *Residual Plot* are not so far away from zero, by standardization, since majority of our values are between 2 and -2; then we are convinced there is a linear relationship between the predictors and the response variable.

* The **Normality assumption was not violated:** Most points follow the *Q-Q line*, with one clear outlier.

* The **Constant Variance assumption was violated:** From the *Residual Plot*, the residual spread is uneven across the predicted values (x-axis), and the large outliers makes it worse. **To fix this (unequal variance): transform the Y (response variable). **Note, this would also serve if normality is violated. We only transform X (i.e. predictor) when "linearity" is violated

## Part 3A: Transform Y (response) using Box-Cox Transformation


```{r, warning = FALSE, message= FALSE}

library(lindia)

gg_boxcox(fit.surgery) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1))  + # Y-axis to 1 dp
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1))   # X-axis to 1 dp

```


### Results 3.1
* The lambda value is $ ~0.1$ with a $95\%$ confidence interval of approximately $-0.1$ and $0.3$. It makes more sense to take $\lambda = 0.0$ for better interpretation in practice.
* Since, $\lambda = 0$, that means our transformation becomes ** $ \ln(Y) $** because:
$$
T(Y) = 
\begin{cases} 
\frac{Y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \neq 0 \\ 
\ln(Y) & \text{if } \lambda = 0 
\end{cases}
$$



## Part 3B: Implement the Transformation of Y (response variable) in the dataset
```{r}
surgery <- mutate(surgery, ln.survival = log(survival))

# check the new column
head(surgery)
```

## Part 4: Data Cleaning -remove the original response variable

```{r}
surgery <- surgery %>% select(-survival)

# check to confirm
head(surgery)

```

## Part 5: Re-fit the model using the transformed Y
```{r}
# use the new response variable to fit the model

fit2.surgery <- lm(ln.survival ~., surgery)
fit2.surgery

```
## Part 6: Model Diagnostics 2
#### Re-check for Linearity, Normality and Constant Variance

```{r}
plot2 <- resid_panel(fit2.surgery, plots = c('resid', 'qq'))

plot2

```

### Results 6.1
* With this transformation, we see from the *Residual Plot* that the residual spread is even across the predicted values (x-axis), and there are no more outliers on the *Q-Q plots*.


## Part 7: BEST MODEL SELECTION
### Using "Best Subset Algorithm" Method

For context on this algorithm:

  * The possible number of models based on our dataset is $2^{(p-1)} = 2^8 = 256$.

  * Where $p =9,$ is the number of parameters (coefficients) in the full model, so, $p-1 = 8$ (intercept excluded)

  * As $p$ increases, so does the multiple-coefficient-of-determination, $R^2$ thus, we should not pick the model with the largest $R^2$.

  * We need the model with the least $R^2$.

  * **GOAL:** Get a leveling off point where adding more variables provides little increase in $R^2$.

```{r}
library(leaps)

select_model <- regsubsets(ln.survival ~ .,
                           data = surgery)


search.models = summary(select_model)
search.models

```
### Results 7.1
* From the established _256 possible models_, the 8 models above are the best model with $n$ predictors.
* For example, the _best model with 3 predictor variables has "prog", "enzyme" and "a.heavy"_


### Which is the best model to use?
* Since $R^2$ will only increase as number of predictors increase, we would expect the model with all 8 parameters to have the highest $R^2$ and model with just "prog" to have the least.
* For this reason, we use the **adjusted R-squared** approach. This adjust more parameters to the regression model.
* Hence, we want the *model with the highest value of adjusted R-square*

```{r}
tibble(predictors = seq(1, 8),
       y = search.models$adjr2) %>%
                                    ggplot(aes(x = predictors, y = y)) +
                                    geom_point() +
                                    geom_line() + 
                                    labs(x = "Number of Variables", y = "Adjusted R-square", 
                                         title = "Best Model by Adj. R-square") +
                                    # theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")) +
                                    theme_bw()
```


#### Check the number of variables that has the highest _adjusted R-Square_ in the graph
```{r}
which.max(search.models$adjr2)

```


### Results 7.2
* **Best Model = model with 6 predictors**
* Thus, our best model, by _Best Subset Algorithm_ will have the following predictors: $blood, \ prog, \ enzyme, \ age, \ gender, \ a.heavy$


## Part 8: Refit the data into a new model 
* Using only the relevant 6 predictors

```{r}
best_model = lm(formula = ln.survival ~ blood + prog + enzyme + age + gender + a.heavy, data = surgery)

best_model
```
## Observation and Next Steps
Although, our predictor variables are less than 30 for this dataset, I would like to test another method called the **Stepwise Regression Method**.


## Part 9: Stepwise Regression Method
For context on this algorithm:

  * When the number of variables is $30$ or more, then _best subset algorithm_ becomes computationally expensive.
  * We will employ the **Backward Stepwise Search** (or simply backward elimination): 
    * This elimination starts with the full model (all predictors) and then removes one variable at a time in the model. 
    * It compares models using numerical criteria such as "AIC" (Akaike Information Criteria). The lower the better.
  
#### Using Backward Elimination

```{r}
backward_elim <- step(object    = fit2.surgery,
                      direction = "backward")
```

### Result 9.1

* The reduction stopped at 6 variables
* This implies that our BEST model is with the following predictors: $blood, \ prognostic \ index \ (prog.), \ enzyme, \ age, \ gender, \ heavy \ alcohol \ user \ (a.heavy)$
* **These predictors are the same the predictors we got when we used the Adjusted R-squared criteria.** Hence, the same _"best model."_

## Part 10: Model Diagnostics 3
#### Check for multicollinearity of our _"Best Model"_
* Using the Variance Inflation Factor $$VIF_{i} = \frac{1}{1 - R_{i}^{2}}$$
* \(VIF_{i}\): The Variance Inflation Factor for a specific independent variable \(X_{i}\).
* \(R_{i}^{2}\): The coefficient of determination (R-squared value) obtained by regressing that specific independent variable \(X_{i}\), against all other independent variables in the model.


* VIF is interpreted as:
  * $VIF = 1$: The variable is _completely uncorrelated_ with other variables
  * $1 \leq VIF \leq 5$: The variable is _moderately correlated_ with other variables
  * $VIF > 5 \ or \ 10$: This is "severe multicollinearity". The coefficients for these variables may be poorly estimated, unstable, and difficult to interpret.


```{r, warning = FALSE, message= FALSE}
library(car)

vif(best_model)


```
### Result 10.1
There are **no significant multicollinearity** in our model's predictor variables. Hence, **a good model.**
